extracted.intended_audience: journalists, media professionals, and readers interested in media ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for how journalists (or public commentators) should respond when accused of lifting others' copy, including corrections, explanations, and avoidance of common excuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prompt response to the charge of plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: She responded promptly to the charge of plagiarism when confronted by the Huffington Post and Politico.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond quickly when confronted; many accused plagiarists go into hiding or deny the charge, which is worse. Prompt engagement is a mitigating, commendable action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amend the work and publish a correction quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: She and her paper quickly amended her column and published a correction (although the correction is a little soft for my taste).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish corrections swiftly and transparently. Corrections should be explicit and substantive enough to address the error; weak or mealy corrections may not satisfy readers or peers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a plausible explanation of how it happened
rubrics_metrics.description: Her explanation of how the plagiarism happened seems plausible—if a tad incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer a believable account for how the material entered the piece, but strive for completeness; partial explanations leave unanswered questions and undermine credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use the explanation as an excuse or say 'time to move on'
rubrics_metrics.description: She’s not yet used the explanation as an excuse, nor has she said it’s 'time to move on.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid framing the explanation as an excuse or demanding people move past the incident quickly. Minimizing or rushing can appear evasive and aggravate critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not protest that the lifting wasn't plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: She’s not yet protested that her lifting wasn’t plagiarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from denying that the copied passage was plagiarism when evidence is strong; denial tends to worsen the situation and damage credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept responsibility and take the consequences without whining
rubrics_metrics.description: She’s taking her lumps and not whining about it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Own the mistake and accept repercussions gracefully. Public contrition and accountability are preferable to defensiveness or victim posturing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid common cop-outs/excuses
rubrics_metrics.description: Many a plagiarist in the past has blamed his theft on over-work, a sick child at home, alcohol use, mental illness, workplace harassment, or a dying parent in the hospice. Others have blamed the sticky cut-and-paste function of their word processors or claimed the words that they copied weren’t that unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on familiar excuse narratives (overwork, family crises, technical features, lack of uniqueness of phrasing, or lack of deliberate intent). Such explanations are viewed skeptically and do not absolve responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that carelessness or lack of intent is not a defense
rubrics_metrics.description: She appears to understand that neither carelessness nor intent constitutes a plagiarism defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand and acknowledge that both negligent and deliberate copying are treated as plagiarism; claiming accidental copying is not a reliable defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give a detailed public account of how the transgression occurred
rubrics_metrics.description: The best and perhaps only way for Dowd to set things right will be to proceed directly to Step 7 and tell her readers in detail how she came to commit this transgression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a thorough, transparent narrative (e.g., in a follow-up column) explaining circumstances, source of the passage, and steps taken to remedy the error. Partial or vague accounts leave lingering distrust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctly attribute the discovery and update errors transparently
rubrics_metrics.description: Correction, May 18, 2009: This article originally attributed the discovery of the Dowd plagiarism to Talking Points Memo. The discovery was made by a reader/blogger posting at the site’s community site, tpmcafe.com. (Return to the corrected sentence.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When initial reports are incorrect about who discovered the issue or other facts, issue clear corrections that state the original error and the accurate information. Track and notify readers of corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware that professional punishment is uneven
rubrics_metrics.description: Punishment [for plagiarism] is uneven, ranging from severe to virtually nothing even for major offenses. The sin itself carries neither public humiliation nor the mark of Cain. Some editors will keep a plagiarist on staff or will knowingly hire one if talent outweighs the infraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that consequences vary widely in the profession; this shapes realistic expectations about outcomes but does not excuse failing to follow best practices for response and correction.
